newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless rate rises to 5 percent as labor market slackens.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless rate rises to 5 percent as labor market slackens.

text.p: The labor market slackened a bit in June as the unemployment rate rose to 5 percent and job growth slowed in the private sector, the government said on Thursday.

The Labor Department report sparked a rally on Wall Street as investors saw no evidence of looming inflationary pressures that might make Federal Reserve policy-makers regret their decision on Wednesday to hold interest rates steady.

"The picture painted by this and other data is clearly one of moderate growth and low inflation," said economist Richard Berner of Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh. "It's a perfect environment for financial markets and for static monetary policy."

After dropping to a near 24-year low of 4.8 percent in May, the jobless rate unexpectedly bounced back to 5 percent last month as the ranks of the unemployed rose to 6.8 million from 6.5 million, the department said. The number of job holders fell to 129.4 million from 129.6 million, it said.

The report contained other signs that the job market, while still tight, was slackening. The number of people seeking jobs for 27 weeks or longer -- the so-called long-term unemployed -- and the number of workers who left their jobs involuntarily both rose in June.

Although the department's survey can produce erratic data from month to month, Bureau of Labor Statistics Commissioner Katharine Abraham said the significance of the increase in the jobless rate should not be downplayed.
"It's statistically significant, but I'm not sure how economically meaningful it was," she told a news conference.

The department's more closely watched payroll survey showed the economy created 217,000 jobs in June, up from 166,000 in May. But in the private sector, job growth outside the farm sector slowed to 151,000 in June from 180,000 in May.
Economists said job growth overall in June was probably overstated, though the data were in line with their expectations and just above the average over the past year.
The report, the government's first look at the health of the economy in June, followed other recent signs that growth was slowing from its rapid first quarter pace.

"It's still a very solid job market, but somewhat slacker in June," said economist Allen Sinai of Primark Decision Economics Inc. in Boston. "There's nothing really wrong with the U.S. economy or the job market. It actually is humming along almost ideally."
Financial markets rallied on the news.

The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 100 points to close at a record 7,895.81, while the 30-year Treasury jumped 1-1/8 points, or $11.25 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.62 percent from 6.71 percent on Wednesday. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Fed policy-makers on Wednesday left short-term rates unchanged on growing signs the economy was slowing from its rapid 5.9 percent first-quarter growth rate. Many economists say second-quarter growth slowed to about a 2 percent rate. The central bankers raised rates in March, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to ward off inflation.

Yet, despite the economy's strength, there have been no signs of a pickup in inflation. Average hourly earnings last month rose by 4 cents, the same increase as in May, to $12.22, and were up just 3.5 percent over the past year, the department said.
The June payrolls increase included 58,000 new jobs in the retail sector, as well as gains of 11,000 computer and data processing and 14,000 in engineering and management services.

Of all new jobs, 82,000 came in state and local government, including 49,000 in schools. But the department's June survey came before the end of the school year and did not register the drop in school employment for summer, which translated into job gains after seasonal adjustment, economists said.
The key manufacturing sector has also shown signs of slower growth recently, with stocks of unsold goods piling up and factory orders falling in two of the past three months.
